title: Tablets when prescription and stock use different units (g, mg, micrograms)
blurb: Convert the prescription and the stock into the same unit, then work out the tablets without a thousandfold slip.
question: A person is prescribed digoxin 0.25 mg. The tablets in stock contain digoxin 125 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?

teach.body: Formal rule: want ÷ have only works when both numbers are in the same unit. Plain English: you cannot divide milligrams by micrograms any more than you can divide pounds by pence. Part A deliberately mixes units, for example a prescription in g with tablets in mg, or mg against micrograms. Convert one of them first, then use want ÷ have exactly as normal.
teach.cite: SI unit definitions; Pearson VUE NMC practice papers (oral items)

teach.caption: Each step on the ladder is 1000. Bigger unit to smaller unit: multiply. Smaller to bigger: divide.

teach.h: Worked example: Mrs Begum on a medical ward
teach.body: Aisha Begum, 62, is prescribed digoxin 0.25 mg. The tablets are digoxin 125 micrograms. Units differ, so convert the prescription: 0.25 mg × 1000 = 250 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 250 ÷ 125 = 2 tablets. Sense-check: two 125 microgram tablets make 250 micrograms, which is 0.25 mg. Type 2.

teach.h: Three ways the same item goes wrong

teach.text: mg versus micrograms is a ×1000 step, and moving the decimal point the wrong number of places gives an answer ten times too big or too small. If you get 0.2 or 20 tablets, recount the three places.

teach.h: Which way do I move the point?

items.label: places the decimal point moves per step

teach.body: Converting the bigger unit down (g to mg, mg to micrograms) usually gives whole numbers, which are easier to divide and harder to misplace. Write the converted value on the note board with its unit before you divide. The answer is still a number of tablets: type the number only.

items: Check the units of the prescription and the tablet before any division.
g ↔ mg and mg ↔ micrograms are each × or ÷ 1000.
Convert to the smaller unit, then want ÷ have.
A result like 0.002, 0.2 or 20 tablets means a conversion slip.
Write "micrograms" in full; never abbreviate it on a chart.

summary: You can now spot a unit mismatch between a prescription and a tablet, convert g, mg and micrograms correctly by 1000, and then calculate the number of tablets. You can also recognise a thousandfold or tenfold slip from an implausible answer.

A.q: A person is prescribed levothyroxine 0.1 mg. The tablets available contain levothyroxine 50 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Convert: 0.1 mg × 1000 = 100 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 tablets.

whyNot.2: 0.1 mg was converted to 10 micrograms (point moved two places, not three).
whyNot.3: 0.1 mg was converted to 1000 micrograms (point moved four places).

A.q: A patient is prescribed clarithromycin 0.5 g. The tablets available contain clarithromycin 250 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Convert: 0.5 g × 1000 = 500 mg. Want ÷ have = 500 ÷ 250 = 2 tablets.

whyNot.1: 0.5 g was taken as 5000 mg, a tenfold conversion slip.
whyNot.2: 0.5 g was taken as 50 mg, a tenfold slip the other way.

A.q: A service user is prescribed haloperidol 1.5 mg. The tablets available contain haloperidol 500 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Convert: 1.5 mg × 1000 = 1500 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 1500 ÷ 500 = 3 tablets.

whyNot.2: 1.5 mg was taken as 15000 micrograms, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: 1.5 mg was taken as 150 micrograms, point moved two places.

B.q: A patient is prescribed sodium bicarbonate 2.4 g twice a day. Each tablet contains sodium bicarbonate 600 mg. How many tablets should be given for each dose?
B.why: Convert: 2.4 g × 1000 = 2400 mg. Want ÷ have = 2400 ÷ 600 = 4 tablets for each dose. Twice a day is the frequency, not part of the single-dose sum.

whyNot.1: 2.4 g was taken as 24000 mg, a tenfold slip giving 40.
whyNot.3: 2.4 g was taken as 240 mg, a tenfold slip giving 0.4.

B.q: A person is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms. The tablets available are labelled digoxin 0.0625 mg. How many tablets should be given?
B.why: Convert: 0.0625 mg × 1000 = 62.5 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 62.5 ÷ 62.5 = 1 tablet. The label and the prescription are the same dose written in different units.

whyNot.1: 0.0625 mg was taken as 6.25 micrograms, a tenfold slip giving 10.
whyNot.2: 0.0625 mg was taken as 625 micrograms, a tenfold slip giving 0.1.
whyNot.3: No conversion: dividing micrograms by mg gives 1000.

B.q: A person is prescribed aspirin 0.3 g. The dispersible tablets available contain aspirin 75 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
B.why: Convert: 0.3 g × 1000 = 300 mg. Want ÷ have = 300 ÷ 75 = 4 tablets.

whyNot.1: 0.3 g was taken as 3000 mg, a tenfold slip giving 40.
whyNot.2: 0.3 g was taken as 30 mg, a tenfold slip giving 0.4.

C.q: A patient is prescribed a medicine 1.5 g a day in three equal doses. The tablets available contain 250 mg each. How many tablets should be given for each dose?
C.why: Convert: 1.5 g = 1500 mg a day. One dose = 1500 ÷ 3 = 500 mg. Tablets = 500 ÷ 250 = 2 tablets per dose.

whyNot.0: This is the number of tablets for the whole day, not each dose.
whyNot.2: 1.5 g was taken as 15000 mg, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: Inverted fraction for the single dose: 250 ÷ 500.

C.q: A person is prescribed levothyroxine 0.175 mg. Levothyroxine 50 microgram and 25 microgram tablets are in stock. What is the fewest number of tablets that gives the dose exactly?
C.why: Convert: 0.175 mg = 175 micrograms. Three 50 microgram tablets make 150 micrograms, plus one 25 microgram tablet makes 175. Fewest = 4 tablets.

whyNot.0: All 25 microgram tablets gives 7 tablets: correct dose, but not the fewest.
whyNot.1: 50 microgram tablets alone give 3.5, which is not a whole number of tablets.
whyNot.3: Two 50s and three 25s make 175 micrograms, but in more tablets than needed.

C.q: A person is prescribed a medicine 0.015 g. The tablets available contain 5 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
C.why: Convert: 0.015 g × 1000 = 15 mg. Want ÷ have = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 tablets.

whyNot.2: 0.015 g was taken as 150 mg, a tenfold slip giving 30.
whyNot.3: 0.015 g was taken as 1.5 mg, a tenfold slip giving 0.3.

reteach.title: Convert, then divide
reteach.question: A prescription says 0.5 mg and the tablets are 250 micrograms. What do you do first?

blocks.body: Change the bigger unit into the smaller one. 0.5 mg × 1000 = 500 micrograms. Now both are micrograms, so 500 ÷ 250 = 2 tablets.

blocks.text: Dividing 0.5 by 250 without converting gives 0.002 tablets: an impossible answer that signals mixed units.

explain.body: Read the unit after each number. If one says mg and the other says micrograms, or one says g and the other mg, you must convert before dividing.

test.q: A person is prescribed 750 micrograms of a medicine. The tablets available contain 0.25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Convert the tablet: 0.25 mg = 250 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 750 ÷ 250 = 3 tablets.

whyNot.0: No conversion: dividing micrograms by mg gives 3000.
whyNot.2: 0.25 mg was taken as 25 micrograms, a tenfold slip giving 30.

test.q: A patient is prescribed a medicine 1.2 g. Each tablet contains 400 mg. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Convert: 1.2 g × 1000 = 1200 mg. Want ÷ have = 1200 ÷ 400 = 3 tablets.

whyNot.2: 1.2 g was taken as 12000 mg, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: 1.2 g was taken as 120 mg, a tenfold slip.

explain.body: 0.125 mg against 62.5 micrograms: convert the mg to micrograms (125) and divide: 125 ÷ 62.5 = 2. Working in the smaller unit keeps the numbers recognisable.

test.q: A person is prescribed digoxin 0.125 mg. The tablets available contain digoxin 62.5 micrograms each. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Convert: 0.125 mg × 1000 = 125 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 125 ÷ 62.5 = 2 tablets.

whyNot.1: 0.125 mg was taken as 1250 micrograms, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: 0.125 mg was taken as 12.5 micrograms, a tenfold slip.

test.q: A patient is prescribed furosemide 0.06 g. The tablets available contain furosemide 20 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Convert: 0.06 g × 1000 = 60 mg. Want ÷ have = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 tablets.

whyNot.2: 0.06 g was taken as 600 mg, a tenfold slip giving 30.
whyNot.3: 0.06 g was taken as 6 mg, a tenfold slip giving 0.3.
